items.description: Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time, checked against the original's recorded behavior at every step. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries in TypeScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby and Java.
items.readme:
rust-anything

Rewrite your whole app in Rust. Keep it working the whole way.

CLIs, servers and libraries, piece by piece, checked against the original at every step.

up to 20x faster · 38,251 recorded cases replayed · 0 mismatches · one command

**Rewrite your whole app in Rust, one piece at a time.** rust-anything records what your TypeScript/JavaScript, Python, C, Go, Ruby or Java app does today, then checks every piece of the Rust rewrite against that recording before it moves on, until the app is pure Rust. CLIs, HTTP servers and libraries; your coding agent (or you) writes the Rust. It can only catch what the recording covers: see [What it can't catch](#what-it-cant-catch). Only need the slow part fast? Port just that, one hot path at a time: | Real workload, same results as the original | Original | With rust-anything | | --- | ---: | ---: | | x18n's sidebar search, 50,000 keys (TypeScript, Node) | 10 ms per query | **0.5 ms: 20x faster** | | The same search in the browser (wasm, one thread) | 10 ms | **0.95 ms: 11.5x** | | `slugify` over 20,000 strings (Python) | 98 ms | **17x faster** | | `Shellwords.shellescape` from Ruby's standard library, 50,000 values | 88 ms | **11.8x faster** | | `Slugify` over 50,000 strings (Go) | 49 ms | **4x faster** | | `slugify` over 50,000 strings (Java) | 43 ms | **3x faster** |

Measured on 4 cores; every number has a benchmark in [`demo/`](./demo) that first checks the results are identical. Calling Rust once per small function is usually *slower* than a JIT; rust-anything finds the loop worth moving, and moves it. > rust-anything is an independent project, not affiliated with or endorsed by the Rust Project > or the Rust Foundation. "Rust" is a trademark of the Rust Foundation. ## Quick start Paste this into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor or Gemini CLI and let your agent install it: ```text Install rust-anything: run `cargo install rust-anything`, then `rust-anything setup`. Tell me when to restart you. ``` Or yourself: ```sh cargo install rust-anything # from crates.io rust-anything setup # registers it with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and Gemini CLI ``` No Rust toolchain yet? Prebuilt binaries for macOS, Linux and Windows are attached to each [GitHub release](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything/releases), and for JavaScript projects `npm install -g rust-anything` installs the same binary. In Claude Code you can also install it as a plugin (the MCP server and the skill; the CLI above must be on your `PATH`): ```text /plugin install rust-anything --marketplace erkamyaman/rust-anything ``` `setup` adds the MCP server to each agent it finds and installs the workflow skill where the agent reads skills. It keeps your other settings, is safe to run again, and `--remove` undoes it. Then ask your agent, for example: - *"Rewrite this CLI in Rust with rust-anything, end to end, and prove it behaves the same."* - *"This search feels slow. Profile it with rust-anything and move the hot loop to Rust."* - *"Plan a migration of `src/parser/` to Rust with rust-anything; port the first unit and prove it."* - *"Bench the Rust port in `rust/text-rs` against the original and tell me whether to ship it."* ### Works with | Agent | `rust-anything setup` adds | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | MCP server in `~/.claude.json`, skill in `~/.claude/skills/` | | Codex | MCP server in `~/.codex/config.toml`, skill in `~/.codex/skills/` | | Cursor | MCP server in `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | | Gemini CLI | MCP server in `~/.gemini/settings.json` | | Any other MCP client | add `rust-anything mcp` as a stdio server by hand (see [Install](#install)) | Before changing a file that exists, `setup` saves a copy beside it (`.rust-anything.bak`). Or run the steps yourself:

```sh rust-anything profile . -- node bench.mjs # what is hot, and who calls it rust-anything bridge . src/fuzzy.ts --batch fuzzyScore:text # write src/port.rs (or let your agent), then: rust-anything record rust/fuzzy-rs && rust-anything build rust/fuzzy-rs rust-anything diff rust/fuzzy-rs # every recorded case must match rust-anything bench rust/fuzzy-rs # faster? the verdict says rust-anything gate rust/fuzzy-rs # done means this passes ``` rust-anything does not translate code: your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, ...) or you write the Rust. rust-anything supplies what an agent cannot guess reliably: where the time goes, what to port first and in which order, a bridge so the rest of the code calls the Rust with its API unchanged, the exact behavior the port must match, a safe way to ship it, and a gate that says when a port is done. ## Languages | Language | Unit | Bridge | Recorded and replayed by | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | TypeScript/JavaScript | folder or file | napi-rs or wasm-bindgen with a generated binary wire; classes and async included | Node, running the `.ts` sources | | Python | package or module | PyO3 (abi3), direct conversion, typed exceptions | Python, importing the original | | C | `.c` file | `extern "C"` functions with the original names and a header | the original compiled to a shared library, called through ctypes, one fork per case | | Go | package | typed cgo calls and a generated binary wire, in a package with the original API | a generated Go driver, built as its own module | | Ruby | file or folder of module functions | a magnus extension under the original modules | a generated Ruby driver | | Java | package of `public static` methods | typed JNI and a generated binary wire, in wrapper classes with the original methods | a generated reflection driver | | PHP (preview) | folder of functions and `public static` methods | coming next: PHP FFI over a C ABI | whole apps today: `app record`, `app replay` and the front door, for CLIs and servers (`php -S`) | | C# (preview) | folder of `public static` methods | coming next: P/Invoke over a C ABI | whole apps today: `app record`, `app replay` and the front door, for CLIs and ASP.NET servers (`dotnet .dll`) | Every language except C also gets batch classes (`--batch`): the items cross once and stay in Rust, and each call runs over all of them on all cores. The language is detected from the repository (`go.mod`, `pom.xml`, a `.csproj` or `.sln`, `pyproject.toml`, `Gemfile`, `composer.json`, `package.json`, else the most common source files); `--lang` overrides it. Types come from the source: TS types, Python hints, C, Go, Java and C# signatures, Ruby YARD tags, PHP types and phpdoc; untyped parameters used as numbers are inferred as numbers. PHP is in preview: `analyze` plans a PHP app (Composer packages and PSR-4 autoloading, risks such as loose comparison and integer overflow into floats, Composer packages mapped to crates), and a PHP CLI or server can be recorded, replayed and put behind a Rust front door. Porting its units into Rust through PHP's FFI is the next step ([issue #2](https://github.com/erkamyaman/rust-anything/issues/2)). C# is in preview the same way: `analyze` reads `.csproj` projects and their NuGet packages (mapped to crates), resolves `using` directives to folders, and flags what C# does differently (`decimal`, `dynamic`, LINQ's deferred queries, `Task`, `lock`, reflection). A C# CLI or ASP.NET server can be recorded, replayed and put behind a Rust front door; porting units through P/Invoke comes next. ## How it works ``` profile ──> analyze ──> bridge ──> record ──> port.rs ──> diff ──> bench ──> shadow ──> gate where the what to the Rust what the you or every faster? both side done means time goes port first crate and original your agent recorded the by side in this passes wrapper does write it case verdict production ``` The original stays the source of truth: `record` runs it on edge cases (and your own inputs) and saves what it returns or throws; `diff` replays every case against the Rust; nothing ships until they all match and `gate` passes. Callers keep the original API throughout. A whole app goes through the same loop unit by unit, inside a frame that proves the whole program ([Port a whole app](#port-a-whole-app)): ``` analyze --whole-app ──> app record ──> app front-door ──> per unit: the loop above, then app wire ──> app lift shape, every what the app Rust owns the gate passes, so the unit answers in pure Rust, dependency, the does from the entry point; the Rust: replay 100%, fallback rate down proved by decisions to make outside original answers replay ``` ## The loop | Step | Command | What it does | | --- | --- | --- | | 0. Profile | `rust-anything profile -- node bench.mjs` | Runs a real workload under the language's profiler (node, cProfile, `go test` pprof, JFR, a Ruby tracer): hot functions by inclusive time, their callers, and which loops to batch; flags code that is already compiled (numba, Cython, JAX), where Rust gains little | | 1. Plan | `rust-anything analyze ` | Units, port order, risks with `file:line`, bridge per unit, dependency-to-crate fit, best first ports; `--whole-app` adds entry points and shape, every dependency (imported or declared) with its crate, pieces (units that import each other move together) and numbered decisions with a recommended answer | | 2. Bridge | `rust-anything bridge ` | Crate with the bindings (`lib.rs`, plus the wrapper the source language loads) and stubs to port (`port.rs`); `--batch fn:param` adds a class that keeps many `param` values in Rust | | 3. Record | `rust-anything record ` | Runs the original on generated edge cases (non-ASCII, emoji, `-0`, `NaN`, ints where floats are expected, ...) and on every semantic trap in every parameter (string length and case, signed division, overflow edges, float printing, map and sort order), and saves `cases.jsonl`; `--float-tolerance 1e-9` lets floats match within that share for numeric code | | 3. Build | `rust-anything build ` | Builds the Rust side: `.node`, wasm package, Python extension or shared library | | 3. Diff | `rust-anything diff ` | Replays the recorded cases against Rust, called the way the original's callers call it; lists mismatches | | 3. Bench | `rust-anything bench ` | Times the recorded cases on the original and on Rust, bridge included | | 4. Shadow | `rust-anything shadow ` | Drop-in that runs both, returns the original's result, reports mismatches; `RUST_ANYTHING_MODE=old\|shadow\|new` | | 5. Gate | `rust-anything gate ` | fmt, clippy `-D warnings`, tests, `unsafe` audit, nothing unported, a recorded failing case for every error path of the original, no `unwrap`/`expect`/`panic!` where the original returns an error (unless marked `// INFALLIBLE: `), build, API, behavior | | Agents | `rust-anything setup` | Registers the MCP server (`rust-anything mcp`, every step as a tool) and the workflow skill ([`skills/rust-anything/SKILL.md`](./skills/rust-anything/SKILL.md)) with your coding agents | ## Port a whole app The goal is a pure Rust app that behaves like the original, with the original kept as reference. Your agent writes the Rust; rust-anything orders the work, scaffolds it, and proves every step. The [whole-app skill](./skills/rust-anything/whole-app.md) walks the agent through it, starting with the decisions only you can make: - **Grilling**: the agent asks in rounds, each question with its recommended answer, until every decision the port depends on is settled, and writes each one as an ADR in `rust/DECISIONS.md`, with `rust/GLOSSARY.md` mapping the original's terms to Rust names. - **Research**: background agents read each dependency's primary sources and write `rust/research/.md`, with every semantic trap they found. - **Across sessions**: `rust/MAP.md` lists every unit with its state; a session claims one unit before it starts, and each checkpoint leaves a `rust/HANDOFF.md` for the next session. Units in one wave can be ported in parallel by subagents. - **Cutover**: the agent does what it can and writes `rust/cutover.sh`, an interactive script for the steps only you can do (deploys, DNS, secrets), with a way back at each step. Grilling, research and these practices are adapted from [Matt Pocock's skills](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills). Plan first: `rust-anything analyze . --whole-app` adds the app's shape (CLI, server or library) and entry points, every external dependency (imported or declared) with its Rust crate and fit, the port order as pieces (units that import each other move together), and numbered decisions with a recommended answer: keep units, blocked units, dependencies with no or a partial crate. Then prove the whole program from the outside. `record` and `diff` prove one unit; `app record` and `app replay` prove the app, for CLIs and servers in any of the six languages (the app is a black box): ```sh rust-anything app record . -- python3 cli.py # the command that runs the original rust-anything app replay . # the original must pass 100% rust-anything app replay . --build "target/release/mytool" ``` - `app record` runs the original on the app's own documented examples (`$ mytool ...` lines in its Markdown and shell files, with the files they name), an `--inputs` JSONL file (`{"name", "args", "stdin", "env", "files"}`), and semantic traps derived from those cases (non-ASCII and emoji strings, negative division and modulo, overflow, large and tiny floats, map order, missing files). Each case runs twice; what differs between the two runs becomes a `[..]` wildcard. `--normalize timestamps|uuids|key-order` or `--normalize name=regex` adds normalizers, saved with the cases. - Cases are [trycmd](https://docs.rs/trycmd) files in `rust/app-cases/`: `.toml` (argv, env, exit code), `.stdin`, `.stdout`, `.stderr`, `.in/` (files in) and `.out/` (files written). Read and edit them by hand; a Rust test can run them with `trycmd` once the port has a binary. - `app replay` runs any build against the cases, prints `passed/total`, writes `rust/app-cases/replay-report.md` with a diff per failing case, and exits non-zero on any mismatch. A build that appends to the file named by `RUST_ANYTHING_FALLBACK_LOG` (one line per fallback to the original), as the front door below does, also gets its fallback rate reported. - `app replay --case ` reruns one case by the name the report gives it: the fast, repeatable loop for fixing a mismatch before running everything again. Then move the entry point to Rust and hand it commands one unit at a time: ```sh rust-anything app front-door . # rust/app: every command runs the original rust-anything app wire . textkit --command upper # after textkit-rs passes gate # write the glue in rust/app/src/units/textkit.rs, then: rust-anything app wire . textkit # 100% again, lower fallback rate ``` - `app front-door` scaffolds `rust/app`, a Rust binary named after the app: a clap parser for the commands and flags in the recorded cases, where every command runs the original with the same argv, stdin and environment and passes its output and exit code through. Each fallback is counted, so replaying the fresh front door gives 100% passed at 100% fallback (it builds and replays to show it). It never overwrites `rust/app`: the code is yours from then on. - `app wire --command ` runs `gate` on the unit crate (`--skip-gate` if it just passed), adds it to `rust/app` as a library, writes `src/units/.rs` once for you or your agent to fill in (parse the arguments, call `::port`, print what the original prints), routes the commands to it, then builds and replays. `RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_=original` sends a wired unit back to the original until the lift. Wire the app's own name as a command (`--command mytool`) for argv that names no command: no arguments, unknown commands, usage errors. When replay passes with fallback rate 0 and every unit passes gate, make it a pure Rust app: ```sh rust-anything app lift . ``` - `app lift` refuses until both hold, and says what blocks it: the cases still falling back, glue still a stub, units failing gate. - On a copy first, it removes the fallback path and the kill switches, turns each unit crate into a plain library of `rust/app` (no `cdylib`, bindings or generated wrappers), and adds `rust/app/tests/app_cases.rs`, which runs `rust/app-cases` with trycmd on `cargo test`, so CI needs nothing but cargo. - Then it runs the lift checklist: fmt, clippy `-D warnings` and tests on every unit and on `rust/app`, every target named in `rust/DECISIONS.md` built or checked where it is installed, files read at run time and asset folders not embedded, and replay on the pure binary. Only when all of it passes are the changes written back. The original is never touched. ### Servers The same commands prove HTTP servers. `--http` says the command starts a server; it takes its port from `PORT` or `{port}` in the command (`--port` for one that always listens on the same port): ```sh rust-anything app record . --http -- node server.js rust-anything app replay . rust-anything app front-door . # axum: every route proxied rust-anything app wire . api --route 'GET /users/{id}' --route '*' rust-anything app lift . ``` - Requests come from `curl` lines in the app's docs (`curl -X POST -d ... http://localhost:8080/x`), `--inputs` (`{"name", "method", "path", "headers", "body"}`) and traps: path segments and query values swapped for the same traps as CLI arguments, bodies for text and JSON traps, and an unknown route. Each run starts the server fresh and sends the requests in name order, so state between requests is kept. - Cases are `rust/app-cases/http/.toml` (the request, the status and the headers that matter) and `.body` (the response body, with `[..]` where two runs differed). Date, server and other per-response headers are left out; delete any header line you do not care about. - The front door is an axum server that starts the original on a port of its own and proxies every route no unit answers. `wire --route` takes axum routes: `METHOD /path/{param}`, `/path` for any method, `*` for everything else; the glue gets the route, its parameters and the request. `lift` removes the proxy; HTTP cases then run in CI with `app replay`. ### Libraries A library has no process to replay: its public API is the front door, and each unit's recorded cases are the proof. ```sh rust-anything app front-door . # rust/app: a Rust crate with the public API # each unit through the loop: bridge, record, port.rs, build, diff, gate; then: rust-anything app wire . textkit-rs # re-exported from rust/app; the original imports its shadow rust-anything app replay . # every wired unit's cases; fallback = exports still in the original rust-anything app lift . ``` - `app front-door` finds the public API (every unit's exports) when the repository has no `main` and no server (`--library` otherwise), and scaffolds `rust/app` as a library crate. Each wired unit becomes a module of it: `pub use textkit_rs::port as textkit;`. - `app wire` takes a crate made by `bridge`, runs `gate`, and writes the unit's shadow drop-in: the original package imports it in place of the unit, so its callers keep the original API and reach the Rust. `RUST_ANYTHING_UNIT_=original` sends the unit back (C: build without the shadow's flags). - `app replay` runs every wired unit's recorded cases through its bindings. The fallback rate is the share of public exports Rust does not answer yet: unwired units, and exports `bridge` keeps in the original language. - `app lift` needs fallback 0 and every unit through `gate`; it strips the bindings, wrappers and shadows from the units and leaves `rust/app` as one pure Rust library. It does not touch any `port.rs`, so the cases that matched through the bindings still describe it; the checklist warns about files of the original that still import the shadows. All five are MCP tools too: `app_record`, `app_replay`, `app_front_door`, `app_wire` and `app_lift`. ## Case study: x18n's core All 29 functions of x18n's core that can move without an API change were ported with rust-anything: every gate passes and 7,925 recorded cases match exactly. `rust-anything bench` then showed the ports are slower than the TS as called from JS, because the bridge costs more than the work. Full report: [`demo/x18n-core`](./demo/x18n-core/README.md). The lesson is built in: measure with `bench` before shipping a port. ## Hot paths: keep the data in Rust A port called once per item pays the bridge once per item, and loses to a JIT. What wins is moving the loop: `profile` finds it, and `--batch` generates a class that takes the items once and runs the function over all of them per call, on all cores, with typed-array results. ```sh rust-anything profile ../x18n -- node --experimental-strip-types $PWD/demo/x18n-search/search.ts . # -> fuzzyScore: a quarter of the run, called per key by `matched`: batch it rust-anything bridge ../x18n packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts --batch fuzzyScore:text ``` ```js const search = new FuzzyScoreBatch(keys) // once const order = search.rank(query, 0) // per keystroke: indexes, best first ``` A `FuzzyScoreIndex` struct in `port.rs` replaces the default loop with one that prepares the items once, and can rank by itself (`rank`): it keeps the keys lowercased with a character mask each, a table of each key's first position of every common character (a one-letter query is one column), and the last query's matches (typing `se` after `s` rescores only what `s` matched). On x18n's sidebar search over 50,000 keys, typed letter by letter, with identical results: | | Per query | vs TS | | --- | ---: | ---: | | TS: `map(fuzzyScore)`, filter, sort | 10 ms | 1x | | TS with the same narrowing as the index | 4.1-5.4 ms | 2x | | The same port, called per key | - | 0.2-0.4x | | `FuzzyScoreBatch`, default index (4 cores) | 5.1 ms | 1.7x | | `FuzzyScoreBatch` with `FuzzyScoreIndex` (napi, 4 cores) | 0.45-0.56 ms | **18-22x** | | The same with wasm (one thread) | 0.95 ms | **11.5x** | Against TS doing the same narrowing, Rust is still 7-12x faster (wasm 5x). Turn the returned indexes into keys with a plain loop: `Array.from(order, i => keys[i])` cost 20x more, 0.4 ms. Every language gets batches, and they beat the original even where per-call ports lose. The same work on 4 cores, identical results and errors (benchmarks in each demo folder): | Language | Workload | Original | Per-call port vs original | Batch vs original | | --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | | TS | x18n search, 50,000 keys | 10 ms | 0.2-0.4x | **20x** | | Python | `slugify`, 20,000 strings | 98 ms | - | **17x** | | Ruby | `slugify`, 20,000 strings | 110 ms | - | **12.7x** | | Ruby | `shellescape` (stdlib), 50,000 mixed values | 88 ms | - | **11.8x** | | Go | `Slugify`, 50,000 strings | 49 ms | 0.93x | **4x** | | Java | `slugify`, 50,000 strings | 43 ms | 0.68x | **3x** | Compiled originals gain less: the per-item work is already fast, so the batch wins by the number of cores. Batch crates allocate with mimalloc: with the system allocator the Go batch was slower than one thread. Demo: [`demo/x18n-search`](./demo/x18n-search/README.md). ## Real code in six languages Go's `path`, Ruby's `shellwords`, Python's `colorsys`, JDK and glibc behavior behind small facades: every port passes its gate, 13,010 recorded cases in all. The runs found and fixed bugs in rust-anything (floats off by one ULP through `serde_json`, C crashes during recording, untyped code getting garbage inputs). Called per function, the Ruby port runs 4.4x faster than Ruby and the Python port 1.35x faster than CPython, while Go and Java leaf functions stay faster in their own language; as batches, all of them win (see the table above). Report: [`docs/real-world-languages.md`](./docs/real-world-languages.md). ## Example: a real module from x18n `packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts` from [x18n](https://github.com/x18n-dev/x18n), ported both ways in [`demo/`](./demo): ```sh rust-anything analyze ../x18n # fuzzy.ts: ready, wasm-bindgen (core runs in browsers) rust-anything bridge ../x18n packages/core/src/fuzzy.ts --out demo/fuzzy-rs rust-anything record demo/fuzzy-rs --count 2000 # write src/port.rs rust-anything gate demo/fuzzy-rs ``` A first port that indexed by Rust `char` passed simple tests but failed `diff`: ``` 198/200 cases match - fuzzyScore("b😀", "a😀b😀c"): expected {"ok":1997}, got {"ok":1998} ``` JS `indexOf` counts UTF-16 code units, so an emoji is two positions. The port in `demo/*/src/port.rs` uses the generated `utf16` helpers and passes 2000/2000 cases and the gate, as napi-rs (`demo/fuzzy-napi`) and as wasm-bindgen (`demo/fuzzy-rs`). The plan rust-anything writes for all of x18n: [`docs/examples/x18n.md`](./docs/examples/x18n.md). ## Install ```sh cargo install --path . ``` `record`, `diff` and `bench` run the original in its own runtime: Node 22.6+ for TS (it runs `.ts` sources directly), Python 3.9+ for Python and C (ctypes), Go 1.21+, Ruby 3+, JDK 17+ (`javac` and `java`). C also needs a C compiler. wasm bridges also need `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown` and `cargo install wasm-bindgen-cli --version --locked`; `build` names the exact version. For agents, `rust-anything setup` registers everything (see Quick start). To add the MCP server to one project by hand instead (`.mcp.json`): ```json { "mcpServers": { "rust-anything": { "command": "rust-anything", "args": ["mcp"] } } } ``` ## What `bridge` decides - Exports that cannot cross a bridge stay in the source language, with the reason, and the shadow module re-exports the original. For TS: functions that take or return functions, generators and iterators, RegExp, `instanceof` checks, generics, and values whose types (followed through imports, re-exports and `extends`) hold functions. `--keep "name: reason"` keeps more, e.g. code that depends on `Intl` data. - TS types map to Rust types, with type aliases resolved through imports and parameter types inferred from default values; structured values cross as a generated binary wire (JSON only as a fallback for shapes the wire does not model). - JSON cannot express `undefined`, NaN, Infinity, -0 or lone surrogates: structured values carry markers (`{"$undefined": true}`, `{"$num": "NaN"}`, `{"$utf16": [...]}`) that the generated `index.cjs` translates, with helpers in the crate's `js.rs`. `record` runs TS sources as they are: a Node resolve hook follows bundler-style imports (`./errors` to `./errors.ts`), `--resolve-from` supplies npm packages when the repo has none installed, and TS that needs transforming (enums, parameter properties) is retried with `--experimental-transform-types`. ## What `analyze` looks at - Packages (`package.json`) and source files; skips `node_modules`, build output, fixtures, playgrounds, tool configs. Vue/Svelte/Astro `

items.name: Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor
items.description: Show the battery level of wireless mice, headsets, keyboards and controllers on the Windows 10/11 taskbar. Lightweight tray app, no vendor software needed. Supports Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, Glorious, PS4/PS5 DualSense, Xbox and Bluetooth devices.

Battery levels of your wireless mouse, headset, keyboard and controller, right on the Windows taskbar.

![Wireless Battery on the taskbar](docs/screenshot.png)

> **Just want it working?** Download **[WirelessBattery-Setup](https://github.com/krisgfx9/Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor/releases/latest)** from the latest release, run it and click through. That's it.
>
> **Experienced users** can grab the portable zip, use the [command-line options](#command-line), or [build it from source](#build) with `make` or `build.bat`.

- **Tiny**: a ~350 KB app using about 2 MB of RAM. It's plain C++/Win32, with no runtime and no background service, and installs in seconds without admin rights.
- **No vendor software needed**: it talks to the devices directly. G HUB, Synapse, iCUE, GG and NGenuity can stay closed (or keep running; they don't conflict).
- **Many brands**: Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, Glorious, Jabra, JBL, PlayStation and Xbox controllers, Samsung Galaxy Buds, any Bluetooth device Windows knows a battery level for, and every headset the bundled [HeadsetControl](https://github.com/Sapd/HeadsetControl) supports.

## Display

**On the taskbar (default):** `🎧 30%  🖱 93%` next to the notification area, drawn with the Windows icon font.
- **Low battery:** a red number means 15% or less.
- **Charging:** a blue ⚡ appears next to the number.
- **Asleep:** dimmed text means the device is asleep and the last known value is shown.
- **Theme:** it follows light/dark mode and DPI scaling.
- **Transparent taskbar themes** (e.g. Windhawk's Taskbar Styler): turn on *Background behind taskbar text* in the menu to keep the text readable over the wallpaper.
- **Several monitors:** the widget shows on every monitor's taskbar, next to its clock, so it stays visible while a game runs fullscreen. *Show the widget on* in the menu picks *All monitors*, *Main monitor only*, or one display (e.g. only *Display 3*).

**Tray icons:** one icon per device with the number drawn in it, plus a "Low battery" notification at 15%. The app switches to this automatically when the taskbar is vertical or can't be found.

Hover for details. Click for the menu: every device (click one to hide or show it), display mode, *Refresh now*, *Start with Windows*, and *Exit*. Levels refresh every 60 seconds, and right away when a device is plugged in or the PC wakes up.

## Install

[![Latest version](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/krisgfx9/Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor?label=latest%20version&style=for-the-badge)](https://github.com/krisgfx9/Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor/releases/latest)

1. Download **`WirelessBattery-Setup-<version>.exe`** from the [latest release](https://github.com/krisgfx9/Wireless-Device-Battery-Monitor/releases/latest).
2. Run it and click through. It needs **no administrator rights** and **nothing else installed**: no
   runtimes, no drivers, no vendor apps. HeadsetControl comes bundled.

The installer adds a Start menu entry and an uninstaller (*Settings → Apps*), and can start the app
when you sign in. Prefer no installer? Download `WirelessBattery-<version>-portable.zip`, unzip it
anywhere and run `WirelessBattery.exe`.

**Notes:**
- **SmartScreen warning:** the exe is not code-signed, so Windows may say "Windows protected your PC". Click *More info → Run anyway*, or build it yourself.
- **Tray-icon mode on Windows 11:** new tray icons go to the `^` overflow. Drag them onto the taskbar or enable them in *Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Other system tray icons*.
- **Keeping the app away from a device:** if a device misbehaves while the app is running, list it in the registry string `IgnoreDevices` under `HKCU\Software\WirelessBattery` as `VID:PID` pairs (hex, separated by commas, e.g. `28BD:0947, 1234:ABCD`; `--dump` shows the ids). The app then never opens it. Drawing tablets are skipped automatically.

## Command line

```
WirelessBattery.exe --list     # print every device and its battery level, then exit
WirelessBattery.exe --dump     # every HID collection, HID devices that could not be opened, all USB devices (also ones
                               # without a HID interface) and Bluetooth devices; also saved to %TEMP%\WirelessBattery-dump.txt
WirelessBattery.exe --report   # open the "Request support for a device" window
WirelessBattery.exe --quit     # close the running instance
```

**Device not shown?** Right-click the widget or tray icon and choose **Request support for a device...**. Pick the device, check
what will be sent (it is shown word for word: the device name, its type, its USB/HID ids and interface layout, and your optional
name and notes) and click **Send**. It goes on the public list at [krisgfx.com/tools](https://krisgfx.com/tools/#requested) and
opens or updates a GitHub issue. **Copy full report** puts the complete `--dump` on the clipboard for the issue. This window is
the only place the app connects to the internet, and only when you click Send.

## Build

You need [MinGW-w64](https://www.mingw-w64.org/), e.g. from [MSYS2](https://www.msys2.org/) (`pacman -S mingw-w64-x86_64-gcc make`).

```
make            # MSYS2 / any shell with make
build.bat       # plain cmd with g++ and windres on PATH
```

To build the installer and portable zip, install [Inno Setup](https://jrsoftware.org/isinfo.php) and run
`powershell -File installer\build-installer.ps1 -Version 1.0.0`. It downloads the pinned
HeadsetControl release and verifies its checksum. GitHub Actions does all of this automatically:
pushing a tag like `v1.0.0` publishes a release with the installer, the portable zip and the
HeadsetControl source (as its GPL license requires).

`WirelessBattery.exe` on its own also works. Without `headsetcontrol.exe` next to it (or on `PATH`) you
just lose the extra headsets.

## Linux (experimental)

A Linux build sits alongside the Windows app. It uses the same vendor drivers with a hidraw-based
HID backend and a GTK4 StatusNotifierItem tray icon; the Windows code path is unchanged.
All Linux-only files are in `linux/` and `src/linux/`, and `build-linux.sh` builds it (Windows keeps using `build.bat`).

| | Fedora | Ubuntu / Debian |
|---|---|---|
| Compiler & make | `sudo dnf install gcc-c++ make` | `sudo apt install g++ make` |
| GTK4 + Cairo | `sudo dnf install gtk4-devel cairo-devel` | `sudo apt install libgtk-4-dev libcairo2-dev` |

No extra HID library is needed (hidraw is used directly).

```sh
./build-linux.sh
./build-linux.sh test         # unit test for the HID report-descriptor parser
./wireless-battery --list     # print detected levels and exit
./wireless-battery --dump     # list HID collections
./wireless-battery --quit     # close the running tray instance
```

HID access needs a udev rule, otherwise the app starts but finds no devices:

```sh
sudo cp linux/99-wireless-battery.rules /etc/udev/rules.d/
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules && sudo udevadm trigger
# log out and back in
```

The tray icon works natively on KDE Plasma; GNOME needs an AppIndicator host such as
`gnome-shell-extension-appindicator`. The optional launcher is `linux/wireless-battery.desktop`
(install it plus `linux/wireless-battery.svg` and the binary into `~/.local/`).

Phase 1 covers Logitech, Razer, SteelSeries, Corsair, HyperX, PlayStation, Cooler Master, Glorious,
Finalmouse and the shared Kysona/Pulsar/ATK/G-Wolves protocols. Bluetooth/UPower fallbacks, HeadsetControl and
the remaining vendors are planned follow-up phases.

## Limitations

- **Primary monitor only:** the taskbar widget sits on the primary monitor's taskbar.
- **Crowded taskbars:** with a very full centered Windows 11 taskbar, the app buttons can reach the widget. On Windows 10 the task-button area is narrowed automatically.
- **Phones:** read from a file Phone Link writes for the Start menu companion card, which is not a documented API and may change with Phone Link updates. The phone shows while Phone Link reports it as connected; a card older than 3 hours is shown dimmed. Charging state is not available there.
- **Sleeping devices:** a device that is asleep may not answer. Its last value stays visible, dimmed. Logitech receivers drop sleeping devices from the link, so their last value is kept for 30 minutes.
- **Keychron keyboards:** they only report their battery over Bluetooth (shown via the Bluetooth support). Over the 2.4 GHz receiver the firmware does not expose it. Keychron mice are supported.
- **Baseus AeQur GH02 headset:** the 2.4 GHz dongle (`10D6:4802`, Actions chip) only carries audio, media keys and the chip's firmware-update channel, not the battery. Connect the headset over Bluetooth to see its level (shown via the Bluetooth support when Windows reports one).
- **Rapoo:** supported VT mice push their status, so a refresh can wait up to 4 seconds per matching interface. Sleeping mice may stay dimmed with their last reading for up to 30 minutes. Support is for Nordic 54L report `07` and legacy VT3 Pro `BB`; CH584 report `08`, office MT/M-series mice and other firmware protocols are not covered by this driver.

Support is for Nordic 54L report `07` and legacy `BB` (VT3 Pro, VT1 Pro Max); CH584 report `08`, office MT/M-series mice and other firmware protocols are not covered by this driver.
- **Flydigi:** this driver targets Vader 5 Pro only; Bluetooth and other Flydigi models are not covered. Percentages represent coarse battery levels. The implementation follows SDL and Windows hardware traces; local hardware validation is pending.
- **Not supported yet:** MSI wireless mice and keyboards other than the VERSA 300 ELITE dongle, Razer Kraken headsets and the Barracuda models other than the Barracuda X (2022) on `1532:0550`, HyperX Pulsefire mice and the Xbox Wireless Headset on the Xbox adapter: their battery protocols are not documented. The Xbox Wireless Headset works over Bluetooth. A USB capture from an owner (see CONTRIBUTING.md) is the way to add them.
- **Not supported yet:** MSI wireless mice and keyboards, Razer Kraken headsets and the Barracuda models other than the Barracuda X (2022) on `1532:0550`, other HyperX Pulsefire mice and the Xbox Wireless Headset on the Xbox adapter: their battery protocols are not documented. The Xbox Wireless Headset works over Bluetooth. A USB capture from an owner (see CONTRIBUTING.md) is the way to add them.
- **Other devices:** some 2.4 GHz devices use undocumented protocols and are not supported yet. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for how to help add one.

## How it works

Each vendor driver in [`src/drivers/`](src/drivers) recognises its devices by USB vendor and product ID, and only ever sends read-only battery queries. Unknown devices are never written to. The generic fallbacks (HID battery usage, Bluetooth, XInput, HeadsetControl) only look at devices no vendor driver has claimed.

The taskbar widget is a layered child window of `Shell_TrayWnd`, placed left of `TrayNotifyWnd`. If Explorer restarts, it is re-created.

items.description: Leonida Is A Native PC Recompilation Of The Xbox Version Of Grand Theft Auto 6
items.readme:
Leonida

Grand Theft Auto VI (Xbox Series) running natively on Windows, built on your PC from your own copy.

Status | How to build | How it works | Want to help? | Credits | License | Discord

Leonida is a static recompilation project. The Xbox Series CPU is x86-64 like a PC, so the game's code is loaded and run natively, and the console's system software is reimplemented. The console's precompiled RDNA2 GPU programs are translated to SPIR-V for Vulkan. The game's models, textures and audio are read from your package. All of this happens **on your PC, from your own copy of the game**. > [!IMPORTANT] > This repository **does not contain the game, keys or an executable**, and it does not explain how to get them. You > need your own copy, with its files already readable on disk. Nothing here decrypts or works around any protection. > Everything the build creates (the generated shaders, extracted assets, the runtime folder and your saves) comes > from your game and stays on your PC. Never share those files. Discord: https://discord.gg/rexed
## Project status **Early. The game does not boot yet.** Everything that can be done without the game's executable is in place, so work on booting can start as soon as one is available to a developer. | What | Status | |---|---| | Finding and checking your copy (Xbox Series 1.0.2.1) | ✅ Works | | Shaders: carve, unpack native RDNA2 code, disassemble | ✅ All 26,503 | | Shaders: RDNA2 → SPIR-V translation | ✅ **All 26,503**: 2,236 VS, 12,101 PS, 2,689 CS, 9,282 mesh, 195 geometry. All pass `spirv-val`, with a per-shader metadata index for pipeline creation. ⚠️ 21,545 are wave64: exact on 64-wide subgroups (AMD), and cross-half wave ops are approximate on 32-wide (NVIDIA) | | Shader translator checked on a real GPU | ⚠️ Vertex fetch, texture sampling, exports, ALU ops, partial-register ops, barycentrics, wave-uniform branches and compute (LDS, barriers, buffer stores) checked on one GPU | | Models (OBJ with real names, UVs, material references) | ✅ Exported. Not all layouts are decoded yet | | Texture dictionaries and world texture pools (DDS) | ✅ Exported. Some pool entries (BCPack) are skipped | | Audio banks (AWC: Opus, XMA2) | ✅ Exported whole. Opus repackaged **losslessly** as Ogg Opus; PCM (codec 0/2) as WAV; XMA2 decoded with ffmpeg. `--wav` adds 16-bit PCM WAV ([notes](docs/audio.md)) | | Music/radio config | ? Measured. **1,589** audio-config records with exact durations and AWC stream ids; station grouping and content-id lists; no per-track start offsets ([notes](docs/audio_config.md)) | | PE loader and import shims | ⚠️ Skeleton. Untested against the real executable | | Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan | ⚠️ In progress. A Vulkan-backed device behind the Xbox-ABI proxy creates queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, views and committed resources; barriers, clears, uploads and copies (BC included) run on Vulkan, checked on one GPU. No shader views, pipelines, draws or swapchain yet ([plan](docs/d3d12_vulkan.md)) | | Booting, story mode, anything playable | ❌ No | ## How to build The port isn't downloaded ready-made. It's built on your PC from your own copy. **The easy way:** 1. Install the prerequisites below. 2. Download this project **with its submodule**: `git clone --recursive https://github.com/ItsNotRexed/Leonida`. A "Download ZIP" from GitHub leaves out `third_party/rpf9-explorer`. The build fetches it if `git` is installed, and otherwise tells you what to do. 3. Double-click **`Build.bat`**. It finds your copy of the game by itself: it looks in Downloads, Desktop, Documents, Games, your home folder and the top of every drive, two folders deep. It recognises the version from a few file sizes, without reading anything large. If you have more than one copy it asks which one, and if it finds none it asks you to paste the folder. Before starting it checks that everything below is installed and that there is enough free space, and it lists anything missing in one go. The result goes to `Documents\Leonida`. A stopped build continues where it left off. Your game folder is the one that holds `MicrosoftGame.Config` and the `.rpf` archives, as plain files. **Prerequisites:** - **Your own copy** of the Xbox Series package, version 1.0.2.1. - **Windows 10/11 x64**, with about **350 GB** free for work files. They can go on another drive with `--work`. - [Python 3.11+](https://www.python.org/downloads/) (tick "Add python.exe to PATH"). - [.NET 8 SDK](https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet/8.0). - [Vulkan SDK](https://vulkan.lunarg.com/), for `spirv-as` / `spirv-val`. - [LLVM 21+](https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/releases) with the **AMDGPU target** for `llvm-mc`. The official Windows build has no AMDGPU target. On Windows, `scripts\build_llvm_mc.ps1` builds a native `llvm-mc.exe` with it (no WSL; needs git and the Visual Studio C++ tools below) and sets `LLVM_MC`. Or install `llvm-21` in WSL and set `LLVM_MC` to the whole command, `LLVM_MC="wsl -d Ubuntu -e /usr/lib/llvm-21/bin/llvm-mc"` (see [docs/design.md](docs/design.md#disassembling-shaders)). On Linux, `llvm-mc` on PATH is enough. - Visual Studio 2022 with **Desktop development with C++**, for the runtime stage. - [ffmpeg](https://ffmpeg.org/download.html) on PATH (optional: decodes the XMA2 streams, and required for `--wav`). **From a terminal**, with the same behaviour and more control: ```powershell python -I make_game.py --find # list the copies found on this PC python -I make_game.py --check # check your copy, build nothing python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --out "D:\Games\Leonida" --work "E:\leonida-work" python -I make_game.py --stages shaders,assets # only some stages python -I make_game.py --game "D:\path\to\your\package" --wav # also decode Opus to PCM WAV (large) ``` Stages run in order: `check`, `shaders`, `assets`, `runtime`, `pipelines` (creates every translated shader on your GPU driver and saves a pipeline cache, so the first boot doesn't compile them). The shader translation is the longest step: it runs on `--jobs` processes (half the CPU threads by default). `--wav` is off by default because 16-bit PCM WAV is several times larger than Ogg Opus. It decodes the repackaged Ogg Opus streams to `work\assets\audio\wav` after the audio bank step; existing WAV files are skipped when a build resumes. ### Vulkan diagnostics on Linux With CMake 3.24+, a C++20 compiler, and Vulkan development headers and loader installed: ```sh cmake -S runtime -B runtime/build/linux cmake --build runtime/build/linux --parallel ./runtime/build/linux/vk_pipeline_check /path/to/spirv ``` Pass the directory containing `index.json` and the translated SPIR-V files to `vk_pipeline_check`. ## How it works | Piece | What it does | Where | |---|---|---| | Version check | Every package file's name, size and SHA-256 for each supported version | `game/`, `make_game.py` | | Shader pipeline | Carves DXBC containers from `shaders.rpf` without its encrypted table of contents. Unpacks the `XBCH` → `FSSM` native RDNA2 program, disassembles it with LLVM (`gfx1013`) and translates it to SPIR-V | `tools/shader_carve.py`, `fssm_unpack.py`, `shader_disasm.py`, `rdna2spirv.py` | | Asset export | Finds validated resources inside RPF9 archives and the loose `.ttpf` texture pools | `tools/rpf9dump` (on rpf9-explorer's Core) | | Runtime | Maps the PE image, resolves imports to shims (GDK, XMem, `d3d12_xs`) | `runtime/` | | Research tools | PE/RTTI inspection, raw carving, texture tiling probes, GPU test harnesses | `tools/`, `runtime/test/` | The translator's runtime contract (user SGPRs, push constants, memory model, bindless images, vertex fetch, system values) and all the format notes are in [docs/design.md](docs/design.md); the format, asset, runtime and validation notes are indexed in [docs/README.md](docs/README.md). The Xbox D3D12 plan is in [docs/d3d12_vulkan.md](docs/d3d12_vulkan.md). Audio bank formats and the export tools are in [docs/audio.md](docs/audio.md); [docs/related_projects.md](docs/related_projects.md) records the prior art we may read and the licence limits on it. ## Want to help? The biggest open pieces: - **Compute, mesh and geometry shaders**: their per-stage system-value register layout. - **Xbox D3D12 → Vulkan**: the `d3d12_xs` command list and descriptor heap model. - **Model layouts** the decoder rejects today. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md). Never attach game files, extracted assets or generated shaders to issues or pull requests. ## Credits - [rpf9-explorer](https://github.com/breadbbbb/rpf9-explorer) by breadbbbb: the RPF9 model, texture-pool and AWC decoders used by `tools/rpf9dump` (git submodule). - [Mesa](https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/mesa/mesa) (MIT): GFX10 resource-descriptor layout (`tools/gfx10_formats.json`), and the ACO/RADV rules used as reference for 16-bit results and shader system registers. - [LLVM](https://llvm.org/): AMDGPU disassembler. - Logo: ["Grand Theft Auto VI" icon by SlyDevil](https://www.steamgriddb.com/icon/122618) on SteamGridDB. - [SPIRV-Tools](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/SPIRV-Tools): assembly and validation. Grand Theft Auto and all related names are trademarks of their owners. This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them. ## License GPLv3 (or any later version). See [LICENSE](LICENSE). Third-party code keeps its own license.

# google-ultra 简体中文 | [English](README.en.md) Google One 的 AI Ultra 有个 12 个月免费试用的 offer，任何页面上都看不到，只存在于 Play 结算库（BillingClient）的返回值里。这个脚本把「查 offer → 拉起 Play 收银台 → 确认 0 元 → 开通」串成了一条命令。 原理是借 Google One 自己的进程调 BillingClient，不需要 Xposed，不需要改 APK。 ## 两个版本 **简单版**：一个网页，双击 `web/index.html` 打开，登录 → 绑卡 → 点一下，完事。不用装 Python，不用 root，不用数据线。 **脚本版**：`ultra0.py`，要一台 root 手机和 frida。优点是 offer 从真实客户端取，不依赖浏览器指纹。 先试简单版，不行再上脚本。 ## 能拿到什么 拿到的是 **Ultra 5x，20TB，12 个月 $0**，到期前取消就不用付钱。开通后 Play 订阅页会写「即将扣款 2027-11-17 US$99.99/月」，这是试用结束后的价格，不是现在扣。 30TB 那档（20x）也查得到 offer，但 Play 结算时会二次校验，大部分号会弹「您不符合免费试用条件」。这个脚本不会去点它。 ## 需要什么 一台 root 过的安卓手机，USB 连着电脑。Magisk、KernelSU、APatch 都行，模拟器也行。 电脑上要 Python 3.9 以上，外加两个包： ```bash pip3 install frida ``` adb 用 Android SDK 里的 platform-tools。装好后 `adb devices` 能看到手机就行。没装过的话，Mac 上 `brew install android-platform-tools`，Windows 去下 platform-tools 压缩包，解压后把目录加进 PATH。 手机上要开「开发者选项 → USB 调试」，插上后在弹窗里点允许。 ## 用法 ### 简单版怎么用 源码在 `web/index.html`，单文件，下载后双击就能用，浏览器会打开一个页面： 1. 点「去登录」，用要开的谷歌账号登进去 2. 点「去绑卡」，绑一张卡，卡里留 1 美元就行，试用期间不扣 3. 回页面，点「Ultra 20 TB」那张卡片 跳到 Google 的结算页之后，确认金额是 0，点订阅即可。 不想下仓库的话，也可以直接访问在线版：https://gylive.github.io/google-ultra/web/ ### 脚本版怎么用 先自检一遍环境，它会检查设备、root、frida-server、推送计费模块，还会顺手关掉会拦截 Play 网络的代理和 Clash： ```bash python3 ultra0.py --check ``` 全绿就可以跑号了。 账号写成一个文本文件，一行一个，字段用四个短横线隔开： ``` 邮箱----密码----辅助邮箱----2FA密钥----卡号----有效期----CVC----持卡人----邮编 ``` 后面几项留空也行。刚买的新号一般没有 2FA，那就留空： ``` abc123@gmail.com----mypassword---- ``` 带卡的话： ``` abc123@gmail.com----mypassword--------4242424242424242----10/29----326----ZHANG SAN----97201 ``` 地址不填会默认用 `123 Main St, Portland, OR 97201`，俄勒冈免消费税。 跑： ```bash python3 ultra0.py accounts.txt ``` 单个号也可以： ```bash python3 ultra0.py --account "abc@gmail.com:密码:2FA密钥" ``` 想看结果，开订阅页确认一下： ``` Play 商店 → 头像 → 付款和订阅 → 订阅 ``` ## 它内部干了什么 1. 把账号加到手机（没有就加，有就跳过） 2. 切 Play 账号。切完一定从头像面板读回来核对，对不上直接退出，不会跑到别的号上 3. 启动 Google One，用 Frida 挂进去，`DexClassLoader` 加载计费模块 4. `queryProductDetailsAsync` 查 `g1.play.20tb`，拿回 5 个 offer 5. 挑免费期最长的那个（`eft-12month`，P1Y），在主线程调 `launchBillingFlow` 6. 盯着收银台。看到价格是 0 或者「免费试用 12 个月」才点订阅；看到「不符合免费试用条件」就关掉，绝不点 7. ﻿# mcp-for-blender-pro

### Your Blender scene. Your AI models. One creative workspace.


**An AI assistant for Blender that can inspect your scene, build objects, edit materials, find assets and carry out multi-step workflows—with a visual chat workspace and a built-in Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.**


![Blender 4.2+](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blender-4.2%2B-E87D0D?logo=blender&logoColor=white)
![Release 1.0.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/release-1.0.0-98D85B)
![Windows x64](https://img.shields.io/badge/download-Windows_x64-357EC7)
![MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)


[Download](https://github.com/bookwjitchieni1986/blender-ai-mcp-addon/releases/latest) · [Getting started](docs/QUICKSTART.md) · [Connections and agents](docs/CONNECTIONS.md)


![AI chat workspace with a live Blender scene preview](docs/images/studio.png)


## Turn a creative brief into scene operations


Start with an idea. Ask the assistant to inspect your scene, create a product-display layout, arrange objects, assign materials or prepare an export. Follow its actions in the conversation and inspect the result in the viewport preview. Keep working in Blender throughout the process.


**mcp-for-blender-pro brings conversation, scene tools, model choice and agent workflows together.** It is designed for artists who want faster iteration, technical artists who automate repetitive work, and developers connecting AI tools to Blender.


## Why choose mcp-for-blender-pro?


| Capability | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| **Blender-aware assistance** | Scene and object inspection gives the assistant context before it acts. |
| **A visual Studio workspace** | Chat, scene objects, viewport snapshots, approvals and a task board in a companion window. |
| **Your choice of AI** | Connect supported cloud providers, local Ollama models or compatible custom endpoints. |
| **Saved connections** | Keep work and personal connections separate, including multiple keys for the same provider. |
| **One assistant or a team** | Use a single model for quick changes, or managers, workers and reviewers for structured tasks. |
| **Built-in MCP server** | Connect OpenCode and other clients supporting authenticated Streamable HTTP MCP. |
| **21 scene tools** | Create, inspect, edit, capture, search assets, consult Blender APIs and export scenes. |
| **Multilingual menus** | Choose English, German, French, Spanish or Chinese for the main interface. |


## From a quick edit to an agent team


Use **Single assistant** for direct, conversational work. For larger tasks, configure a **Team chain** with individual responsibilities, instructions and models.


- **Manager:** breaks the request into assignments and acceptance criteria.
- **Workers:** perform the assigned scene operations.
- **Reviewers:** inspect results and approve work or return specific findings.


Tasks run sequentially so scene edits stay ordered. A blocked task gets one correction attempt; a second failed review stops the workflow. The task board exposes assignments, attempts and review findings as work progresses.


![Agent roles and model configuration](docs/images/studio-team.png)


## Connect the models that fit your work


Supported connections include **OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, OpenRouter, OpenCode Zen, Ollama and custom APIs**. Load the available model catalog and select a model directly in Blender or Studio.


Custom endpoints support OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages and Ollama protocols. Choose models with tool-calling support; image-capable models can also interpret viewport screenshots. OpenCode-only free models are available through the OpenCode client.


![Provider, saved connection and model selection](docs/images/studio-settings.png)


## Install and create


1. Download **`mcp-for-blender-pro.zip`** from [Releases](../../releases/latest).
2. In Blender, open **Edit → Preferences → Get Extensions → menu → Install from Disk**.
3. Select the ZIP, enable **mcp-for-blender-pro**, then open **3D Viewport → N → MCP Pro**.
4. Choose a provider, add your connection details and select a model.
5. Send a message in Blender or click **Open Studio Window**.


The release bundle targets **Windows x64 with Blender 4.2 or later**. Keep Blender open while using Studio or an external client.


### Try these prompts


> Inspect this scene and explain its object structure before making any changes.


> Create a simple product-display scene with a pedestal, a camera and three lights. Give the pedestal a matte blue material.


> Duplicate the selected object into a neatly spaced row of five and show the viewport.


> Find an appropriate Poly Haven asset for this scene and ask before importing it.


## Blender automation through MCP


Launch **OpenCode Portable** from the sidebar to work through OpenCode with the Blender connection configured for you. OpenCode manages its own provider sign-in and model selection. Other compatible MCP clients can connect to the authenticated local endpoint described in the [connection guide](docs/CONNECTIONS.md).


| Tool group | Included tools |
|---|---|
| Scene inspection | `get_scene_info`, `list_objects`, `get_object_info` |
| Object creation | `add_cube`, `add_sphere`, `add_cylinder`, `add_plane`, `add_light`, `add_camera` |
| Editing | `move_object`, `duplicate_object`, `delete_object`, `parent_objects`, `set_material` |
| Visual feedback and scripting | `viewport_screenshot`, `execute_code` |
| Blender API and export | `bpy_api_lookup`, `describe_node_type`, `export_scene` |
| Asset workflows | `search_assets`, `import_asset` |


Asset integrations include **Poly Haven, Sketchfab and Poly Pizza**. Configure service keys where required and follow the licenses of the assets you use.


## Stay in control of your scene


Built-in chat supports operation approvals, cancellation after the current step and named undo steps for mutations. Python tool validation helps catch disallowed operations; it is not a security sandbox. External MCP clients manage their own approval policies.


Connection credentials are stored in your user settings. Chat history lasts for the current session. Studio runs locally and authenticates requests to Blender.

# ung220z-tool

针对 **UNG220Z（九联 / Unionman 中国移动光猫）** 的一键凭据提取工具。

> ⚠️ 仅用于**你自己的设备**，用于找回自己忘记的管理密码、迁移宽带配置或安全自查。
> 未经授权对他人设备使用属于违法行为，作者不承担任何责任。

## 背景

这类光猫的 Web 管理页基于 `.gch` CGI 框架，登录口令由 TR-069 定期轮换，普通用户拿到的密码往往几天就失效。本工具走 Telnet 通道，直接读取设备配置库，拿到**当下有效**的全部凭据。

## 工作流程

```
用户输入账号密码
   ↓
拼出 http://<ip>/usr=<user>&psw=<pass>&cmd=1&telnet.gch 并打开浏览器（同时脚本直连兜底）
   ↓
Telnet 登录 → root shell
   ↓
sidbg 1 DB decry /userconfig/cfg/db_user_cfg.xml 解密配置
   ↓
提取 Web 账号 / Telnet 口令 / PPPoE / WiFi 密钥 / root 口令
   ↓
打印凭据表 + 落盘日志
```

## 用法

```bash
python3 ung220z.py
```

会依次询问：

```
※ 用户名和密码通常印在光猫【背面贴纸】上（S/N 标签）
  形如「用户名：user   密码：xxxxxxxx」，把光猫翻过来就能看到

① 光猫地址 [192.168.1.1]:
② 用户名 [user]:
③ 密码（输入时不显示）
   密码:
```

也可以全部走命令行：

```bash
python3 ung220z.py -i 192.168.1.1 -u user -p '你的密码'
python3 ung220z.py -i 192.168.1.1 -u user -p '你的密码' --no-browser
```

### 常用参数

| 参数 | 说明 |
|---|---|
| `-i, --ip` | 光猫地址，默认 `192.168.1.1` |
| `-u, --user` | 登录用户名，默认 `user` |
| `-p, --password` | 登录密码，不填则交互输入 |
| `--telnet-user` | Telnet 用户名，默认 `CMCCAdmin` |
| `--telnet-password` | Telnet 口令（部分机型与 Web 口令不同） |
| `--no-browser` | 不调用浏览器，纯 HTTP 请求 |
| `--unlock` | Web 被会话锁占住时重启 httpd 解锁 |
| `--no-release` | 不尝试释放残留 Web 会话 |

## 输出示例

```
[22:15:00] INFO   会话开始  目标=192.168.1.1  账户=user
[22:15:00] HTTP   已发送给浏览器: http://192.168.1.1/usr=user&psw=***&cmd=1&telnet.gch
[22:15:00] HTTP   telnet.gch → TelnetSet Success!
[22:15:00] PROBE  nc -zv 192.168.1.1 23 → succeeded
[22:15:01] AUTH   Telnet CMCCAdmin / ****** → 登录成功（root）
[22:15:02] SHELL  sidbg 1 DB decry /userconfig/cfg/db_user_cfg.xml → /tmp/debug-decry-cfg
[22:15:03] DATA   DevAuthInfo  CMCCAdmin  / ******  Level=1
[22:15:04] CRACK  MATCH: ******  (/etc/shadow)
```

最后输出凭据汇总表，并写入 `ung220z_<时间戳>.log`。

## 依赖

- Python 3.8+
- 标准库即可，无需 pip 安装
- 设备已开启 Telnet（脚本会自动通过 `telnet.gch` 尝试开启）

## 原理说明

| 环节 | 说明 |
|---|---|
| 开 Telnet | `GET /usr=<user>&psw=<pass>&cmd=1&telnet.gch`，返回 `TelnetSet Success!` 即成功 |
| Web 登录 | 密码前端只做 base64，`Frm_Logintoken` 每次响应递增，必须回填实时值 |
| 配置解密 | `sidbg 1 DB decry` 无口令即可解密，得到明文 XML |
| root 口令 | `/etc/shadow` 中为 SHA-256 crypt，工具会用常见出厂口令比对 |

## 免责声明

本项目仅用于教育与自有设备维护。使用者应确保对目标设备拥有合法管理权限。

# NeonClipping

**Paste a link. Get captioned 9:16 clips in about two minutes. Free, local, open-source.**

NeonClipping turns long YouTube / Twitch / Kick videos (or your own MP4) into vertical, captioned clips with a title and hook for each. Everything runs on your machine: no account, no subscription, no upload.

[![Star on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/iamajmeena/neonclipping?style=for-the-badge&logo=github&label=Star%20on%20GitHub)](https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping) [![Instagram](https://img.shields.io/badge/Follow-%40iamajmeena-E4405F?style=for-the-badge&logo=instagram&logoColor=white)](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/)

🌐 **Website with one-click Windows setup:** <https://iamajmeena.github.io/neonclipping/>

**Made by [Ajay K Meena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/)** (Director, DOP, colorist, DaVinci Resolve educator, Jaipur). If NeonClipping saves you time, please ⭐ star the repo and follow [@iamajmeena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/) on Instagram.

![demo](docs/demo.gif)

![UI](docs/neonclipping-ui.jpg)

📘 **Guides (Hindi + English, PDF):** [docs/NeonClipping-Guide-EN-HI.pdf](docs/NeonClipping-Guide-EN-HI.pdf)  
🤖 **Let an AI agent install it for you:** copy [docs/NEONCLIPPING-AGENT-SETUP-PROMPT.txt](docs/NEONCLIPPING-AGENT-SETUP-PROMPT.txt) into Claude Code, Codex CLI or Cursor.

## How it finds good moments

Two modes, one button.

**⚡ Fast mode (default, videos over 10 min)** copies the trick that makes the fastest clippers fast: never look at the whole video.

1. Download **audio only** (79 MB for an 85-minute video, about 10 s).
2. Take the transcript for free from YouTube's own captions (word-timed). No speech model needed. For other sources a local Whisper model is used as the fallback.
3. Score the whole audio track for *sudden loudness jumps* (vs a 2-minute local baseline), *raised voices* (2–4 kHz energy) and quiet-to-loud transitions.
4. Take the best moments, read each one's transcript with a local LLM (Ollama) and let it score the moment, write a title and a hook. Snap the start and end to sentence boundaries inside your Min/Max length.
5. Download **only the chosen sections** of the video (not the whole file), trim exactly by matching their sound to the audio track, and render 1080x1920 clips with burned-in captions.

**🔬 Deep mode** downloads the whole video, adds optical-flow motion (OpenCV Farneback: fast objects, impacts, camera whips) and cut density to the audio signals, shortlists 4× more candidates and gives the LLM 15 seconds of context before and after each one.

Measured on one machine (RTX 2060, 16 threads), Fast mode, 3 clips each:

| Source | Time |
|---|---|
| 85-minute YouTube stream (YouTube captions) | **97 s** |
| 3-hour Twitch VOD (no captions, local speech model) | **136 s** |
| 90-second YouTube trailer | 21 s |
| 90-second local MP4 | 14 s |

Your numbers depend on network and CPU.

## How it decides what is a good moment

Every candidate moment is scored from several signals, then the best ones are kept:

| Signal | What it looks for |
|---|---|
| Loudness jump | A sudden boom or shout compared with the last two minutes |
| Raised voice | Energy in the 2–4 kHz band (screaming, yelling) |
| What is said | "oh my god", "oh shit", "run", "police", "bhaago", "arre yaar" and similar (English, Hinglish, Hindi) |
| On-screen action | Fast motion (optical flow), explosion-like flashes, red/blue light flicker, scene cuts |
| AI score | A small local LLM reads the transcript: emotion, punchline, payoff |

**It learns from you.** Under every clip there are 5 stars. Your ratings stay on your computer (`data/feedback.jsonl`). After 8 ratings the weights of the signals above are re-fitted (ridge regression pulled toward the defaults, blended in gradually), so a gamer-shouting-heavy taste ranks shouting higher and a calm-explainer taste ranks it lower. Nothing is uploaded.

## Features

- One-click **Make clips**, live progress, clips appear one by one with preview and MP4 download.
- **Min / Max clip length** (e.g. 30–80 s). Clips end on a sentence.
- **Facecam position presets** (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, bottom-centre, none) for the usual streamer layouts, remembered between sessions. Or draw the face and gameplay boxes yourself in the editor.
- **11 native layouts:** camera above/below gameplay, blurred fill, full-screen crop, gameplay only, four corner overlays, circle facecam and side-by-side. Independent face/game selection and a face-size slider. Preview-only platform safe zones.
- Caption styles: GTA Neon, Impact, Clean, Hormozi and MrBeast. Word-timed, editable words, SRT export.
- **Hinglish captions**: Hindi speech is written in English letters ("kya haal hai bhai") by default. Pick Hinglish / हिंदी / English explicitly if you like. Caption accuracy: Fast, Accurate (Whisper large-v3-turbo, default) or Best Hindi (large-v3, much slower on small GPUs).
- **Make clips uses your own setup**: facecam preset or the boxes you draw in step 03.
- Optical-flow motion + audio highlight ranking, frame-accurate NVENC export (falls back to x264).
- Nothing leaves your computer. The server binds to `127.0.0.1` only.

## Change clips after generating them

![Saved clip editor with eleven layouts](docs/saved-clip-editor.jpg)

Open **My clips → Edit clip**. The saved editor includes all **11 speaker position/shape layouts**, a speaker-size slider, editable subtitle words, caption style and caption height.

- **Apply to this clip** updates the opened clip.
- **Apply to this video's clips** updates the currently saved clips associated with the same source URL. Each keeps its own timestamps, transcript, title and hook. New clips still being generated are not included in that snapshot.
- Source download, highlight discovery and speech recognition are **not repeated**. Burned-in captions and framing require encoding a new final MP4.
- Original source files must remain in `data/`. Previous MP4s are kept; the library displays the latest versions. Old exports missing saved word timings can recover captions from their SRT, with approximate per-word timing.
- This edits the selected moments; changing the clip's start/end or spoken language requires a separate trim/transcription workflow.

Validation on one 796.9-second source: all 11 layouts and five caption styles exported with audio and decoded successfully. A seven-clip layout/style update took 119.58 seconds while reusing each clip's exact source, range and word list. These are local checks, not guaranteed runtimes or a caption-quality benchmark.

Run the portable regression tests with `python -m unittest discover -s tests -v`.

## Install

**Easiest (Windows):** download [`NeonClipping-Setup.bat`](https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping/releases/latest/download/NeonClipping-Setup.bat) from the [website](https://iamajmeena.github.io/neonclipping/) or the Releases page and double-click it. It checks your PC, installs Python and FFmpeg if missing, installs NeonClipping into `%LOCALAPPDATA%\NeonClipping`, creates a Desktop shortcut and opens the app. Mac/Linux: `install.sh` (new, not yet tested on a real Mac). Or follow the steps below.

Requirements: Python 3.10+, FFmpeg on PATH. Optional but recommended: [Ollama](https://ollama.com) with `ollama pull llama3.2:3b` for AI titles, hooks and scores (without it clips are picked by the audio/motion score), and an NVIDIA GPU for NVENC and faster-whisper.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/iamajmeena/neonclipping
cd neonclipping
# Windows
./run.ps1
# Linux / macOS
./run.sh
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:8770>, paste a link, press **⚡ Make clips**.

Optional GPU speech model support (only used when a video has no YouTube captions):

```bash
.venv/bin/pip install nvidia-cublas-cu12 "nvidia-cudnn-cu12==9.*"
```

Set `NEONCLIPPING_CPU=1` to force CPU. Set `NEONCLIPPING_PORT=9000` to use another port.

## How it is built

| File | Job |
|---|---|
| `app.py` | FastAPI server, `/make` pipeline, export, library |
| `smart.py` | Moment scoring: transcript + local LLM, sentence snapping |
| `highlights.py` | Audio-jump / shout / optical-flow / cut ranking, parallel decode |
| `captions_yt.py` | YouTube word-timed captions (json3) parser |
| `captions.py` | Local Whisper (GPU first, CPU fallback), ASS/SRT styles |
| `translit.py` | Devanagari → Hinglish (word by word, keeps timings) |
| `standalone.py`, `previews.py` | Link import, early preview frames |

## Live clipping (while the stream is on)

Paste a Twitch channel link or a YouTube Live link into the **Live clipping** panel and press Start. NeonClipping records the stream (Streamlink), reads chat anonymously, counts messages in 10 s buckets and cuts a clip around every chat spike (chat velocity more than 2.5 sigma and 2.5x the 5-minute baseline). The clip starts about 24 s *before* the spike, because chat reacts after the moment. It then gets captions, a hook and title, your layout and facecam boxes, and a viral score like any other clip. **Clip the last 30 s now** cuts on demand, **Stop** ends the session. It only works while the stream is live; for finished videos use Make clips.

There is also a command-line version in `live/live_clip.py`.

## Creators (clip a streamer automatically)

Add a Twitch name or a Twitch / YouTube channel link in the **Creators** panel. NeonClipping checks every minute; when that creator goes live it records the stream and clips the chat spikes, using the layout, facecam boxes and caption style you had selected when you added them (“Use my current layout” updates it). Clips appear under the creator and in My clips.

- One stream at a time (recording and rendering are heavy); other creators wait their turn.
- NeonClipping must stay open. Unattended recordings stop after 3 hours (a new one starts if the creator is still live), stop when less than 8 GB of disk is free, and the big recording file is deleted after the last clip is cut.
- Pressing **Stop** pauses that creator for 30 minutes; switching Auto off and on resumes at once.
- Tested on Twitch (recording, chat spikes, clip, feed). YouTube channels are detected through yt-dlp; an auto-clipped YouTube stream was not run end to end.

## Tests

`tests/` holds an end-to-end suite that runs against the live server: page and API validation, every layout and caption style rendered and measured, editing one / all clips of a video, Make clips on real YouTube / Twitch / local sources in every mode and language, live clipping on a real stream, the creator list, star ratings, the installer and the website. Unit tests cover the chat-spike rule, caption grouping and re-editing. The last full run is in [`tests/REPORT.md`](tests/REPORT.md): 187 checks, all passing, plus the 12 problems the run found and fixed.

```
python -m unittest tests.test_captions tests.test_live tests.test_reedit
python tests/e2e.py static export edit creators feedback   # server must be running
python tests/e2e_make.py          # real downloads + transcription (about 25 min)
python tests/e2e_live.py          # needs a Twitch channel that is live
python tests/e2e_site.py          # website, links, release assets
python tests/make_report.py       # rebuild tests/REPORT.md
```

## Style & extras

- **Templates:** wrap the clip in an *X post* (light or dark), a *TikTok hook* box or a *Breaking news* broadcast frame. Type the name, handle and hook; the card, avatar letter, check mark and ticker are drawn for you.
- **Background card:** padded, rounded-corner video card on a blurred copy, a colour, a gradient or your own image (dimmed, blurred).
- **Logo / watermark** (4 corners, size, opacity), **credit line** (or "Clip: channel name" automatically), **outro ribbon** that slides in for the last seconds.
- **Music bed:** one track under the voice that rises to a peak volume in the last seconds (volume, peak and riser length are yours).
- **Six caption animations:** highlight (word by word), pop-in, pop-in line, one by one, build up, full line.
- **Import captions:** drop an `.srt` or `.ass` file; the words are timed to the clip and can be edited.
- All of it works in Make clips, single exports and "Edit saved clips" (including "apply to all clips of this video").

## Find my facecam

The **Find my facecam** chip (or "find it automatically when I press Make clips") looks at 14 frames of the video, finds rectangles whose border stays in the same place, and keeps the one that holds a face (small local YuNet face model, MIT licence, `models/`). It rejects the game's minimap and HUD panels, finds webcams in a corner or floating on a side, and answers "no facecam" when it is not sure. Measured on 30 real saved streams: found the webcam on every stream that has one; clean "not found" on trailers and talking-head videos. Not perfect: some boxes cover only the face inside a framed webcam.

## Long streams with a free chatbot

**AI parts** (below step 01): paste a YouTube link, NeonClipping splits the video's captions into ~25-minute parts and gives a copy-ready prompt per part. Paste each into any free chatbot, paste all answers back (JSON or lines like `12:30-13:10 title`), tick the moments and press Make clips: only those sections are downloaded and rendered. A chatbot given a 9-hour transcript in one go only reads the start; small parts fix that. Nothing is sent anywhere by NeonClipping; the chatbot step is manual.

## Honest limits

- Highlight picking is a heuristic plus a small local LLM. It finds loud, energetic, quotable moments, not guaranteed "viral" ones. Review before posting.
- The action cues (motion, flash, light flicker) are simple heuristics on a tiny low-resolution copy; they rank moments, they do not recognise "a police chase". Star ratings are how it gets better at your taste.
- The LLM sees text only. It cannot see the screen.
- Without YouTube captions (Twitch VODs, uploaded files) a speech model must transcribe each candidate, which is slow on CPU.
- Auto-caption accuracy follows the source: YouTube's auto captions are imperfect, especially Hinglish.
- Deep mode was verified on a short video only; on multi-hour videos it downloads the whole file first and is slow by design.
- Facecam presets are starting points, not detection: if you pick Bottom-right but the cam is bottom-left, the top half of the clip will show the wrong area. Pick the right corner or draw your own boxes.

## Support

NeonClipping is free. If it saves you time you can ⭐ star the repo, follow [@iamajmeena](https://www.instagram.com/iamajmeena/), or optionally donate via Razorpay (UPI / cards): <https://rzp.io/rzp/JN41CpW>. The app also has a ♥ Donate button. Nothing is ever locked behind a donation.

## Credits and inspiration

Design ideas studied from open-source clippers: [PeakCut](https://github.com/haziqahmedqasmi/PeakCut) (audio-first download, captions as transcript, section download), [ClipCutter](https://github.com/curtyo18/ClipCutter), [content-ai](https://github.com/buddah0/content-ai), and the Growlance live-clipper script. Also studied: PeakCut's facecam-by-static-border idea and creator list (reimplemented here with our own code, plus a face check), the public feature list of the YIZERGE desktop editor (templates, background card, music riser, caption animations; only its public web page was read), and a creator's walkthrough of splitting a 9-hour stream into small transcript parts for a free chatbot. Built on FFmpeg, yt-dlp, FastAPI, faster-whisper, OpenCV (YuNet face detector, MIT), Ollama.

## License
